subtopics.title: Coordinate geometry in the (x, y) plane

command_words.Show that: Prove a given result; every step must be shown (answer given).
command_words.Hence: Use the previous result to reach the answer.
command_words.Hence or otherwise: Using the previous result is expected, but any valid method earns the marks.
command_words.Find: Work out; method marks need working.
command_words.Calculate: Work out from given facts; show working.
command_words.Sketch: Draw the shape with key features labelled (intercepts, asymptotes, turning points), not to scale.
command_words.Exact: Give the answer in surd, fraction, pi or ln form, not a decimal.
command_words.Verify: Show that given values satisfy the statement.
command_words.Interpret: Explain the meaning of a result in the context of the question.

kcs.title: Proof by contradiction
kcs.guidance: Including proof of the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ and the infinity of primes, and application to unfamiliar proofs.

kcs.title: Partial fractions
kcs.statement: Decompose rational functions into partial fractions (denominators not more complicated than repeated linear terms).
kcs.raw: Decompose rational functions into partial fractions (denominators not more complicated than repeated linear terms).
kcs.guidance: Partial fractions to include denominators such as $(ax+b)(cx+d)(ex+f)$ and $(ax+b)(cx+d)^2$. The degree of the numerator may equal or exceed the degree of the denominator. Applications to integration, differentiation and series expansions. Quadratic factors in the denominator such as $(x^2+a)$, $a>0$, are not required.

kcs.title: Parametric equations of curves
kcs.statement: Parametric equations of curves and conversion between cartesian and parametric forms.
kcs.raw: Parametric equations of curves and conversion between cartesian and parametric forms.

kcs.title: Binomial series for rational n
kcs.raw: Binomial Series for any rational n.
kcs.guidance: For $|x| < \dfrac{b}{a}$, students should be able to obtain the expansion of $(ax+b)^n$, and the expansion of rational functions by decomposition into partial fractions.

kcs.title: Implicit and parametric differentiation
kcs.statement: Differentiation of simple functions defined implicitly or parametrically.
kcs.raw: Differentiation of simple functions defined implicitly or parametrically.
kcs.guidance: The finding of equations of tangents and normals to curves given parametrically or implicitly is required.

kcs.title: Forming differential equations
kcs.guidance: Questions involving connected rates of change may be set.

kcs.title: Volume of revolution
kcs.guidance: $\pi\displaystyle\int y^2\,dx$ is required, but not $\pi\displaystyle\int x^2\,dy$. Students should be able to find a volume of revolution, given parametric equations.

kcs.title: Integration by substitution and by parts
kcs.statement: Simple cases of integration by substitution and integration by parts. Understand these methods as the reverse processes of the chain and product rules respectively.
kcs.raw: Simple cases of integration by substitution and integration by parts. Understand these methods as the reverse processes of the chain and product rules respectively.
kcs.guidance: Students will be expected to use a substitution to find, e.g. $\displaystyle\int x\sqrt{x-2}\,dx$. The substitution will be given in more complicated integrals. The integral $\displaystyle\int \ln x\,dx$ is required. More than one application of integration by parts may be required, for example, $\displaystyle\int x^2 e^x\,dx$, $\displaystyle\int e^x \sin x\,dx$.

kcs.title: Integration using partial fractions
kcs.statement: Simple cases of integration using partial fractions.
kcs.raw: Simple cases of integration using partial fractions.
kcs.guidance: Integration of rational expressions such as those arising from partial fractions, e.g. $\dfrac{3}{(x-1)^2}$, $\dfrac{2}{3x+5}$. Note that the integration of other rational expressions, such as $\dfrac{2x}{(2x-1)^4}$ and $\dfrac{5}{4x+2}$, is also required (see P3 section 5.2).

kcs.title: Separable differential equations
kcs.statement: Analytical solution of simple first order differential equations with separable variables.
kcs.raw: Analytical solution of simple first order differential equations with separable variables.
kcs.guidance: General and particular solutions will be required.

kcs.title: Area under a parametric curve
kcs.statement: Use integration to find the area under a curve given its parametric equations.
kcs.raw: Use integration to find the area under a curve given its parametric equations.
kcs.guidance: Students should be able to find the area under a curve given its parametric equations. Students will not be expected to sketch a curve from its parametric equations.

kcs.title: Vectors in 2D and 3D
kcs.statement: Vectors in two and three dimensions.
kcs.raw: Vectors in two and three dimensions.

kcs.title: Magnitude and unit vectors
kcs.guidance: Students should be able to find a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{a}$, and be familiar with $|\mathbf{a}|$.

kcs.title: Vector addition and scalar multiples
kcs.statement: Algebraic operations of vector addition and multiplication by scalars, and their geometrical interpretations.
kcs.raw: Algebraic operations of vector addition and multiplication by scalars, and their geometrical interpretations.

kcs.title: Distance between two points in 3D
kcs.guidance: The distance $d$ between two points $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ is given by $d^2=(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2+(z_1-z_2)^2$.

kcs.title: Vector equations of lines
kcs.guidance: To include the forms $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{c}+t(\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{c})$. Conditions for two lines to be parallel, intersecting or skew.

kcs.title: Scalar product and angle between lines
kcs.statement: The scalar product. Its use for calculating the angle between two lines.
kcs.raw: The scalar product. Its use for calculating the angle between two lines.
kcs.guidance: Students should know that for $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b}=b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k}$, then $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3$ and $\cos\angle AOB = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}$. Students should know that if $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$, and $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are non-zero vectors, then $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular.
